items.title: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police
items.summary: South African communities tell the BBC of measures they're taking to keep women safe after a wave of horrific killings.
items.body:
Image source, Family handout

Image caption,

Okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. She had two children, aged three and nine, and was a civil engineering student

ByNomsa Maseko, Thuthuka Zondi and Eleanor Smallwood , BBC World Service, Reporting fromEkurhuleni

Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.

It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.

Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured.

"When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.

After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.

But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.

When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten.

"It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it."

Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBC

Image caption,

Okuhle's father, Tuku, says he feels "ignored and unseen" by the government after his daughter's death

Okuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.

She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September, according to the South African Police Service.

Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.

It is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years as police had stopped releasing this breakdown until now.

There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.

South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.

Am I Next? Fear and Survival in South Africa

The BBC World Service visits communities struggling to confront widespread violence against women

Watch on iPlayer

Viewers outside the UK can watch on YouTube

In response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.

But in places like Kokstad, as well as Kempton Park, in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.

For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.

Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested.

"It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate."

He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.

The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received.

The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South Africa

According to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.

This year, Amnesty International said South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".

Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.

Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change.

"I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us."

Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.

Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".

Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBC

Image caption,

Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00

Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.

Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.

In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.

Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.

Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.

The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu.

Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up.

Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers.

"With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do."

Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.

Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBC

Image caption,

Kgothatso says she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap her

Kgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempton Park.

She was in a taxi when the driver locked the doors and started driving in the wrong direction.

When Kgothatso told him he had missed the turn, she says he started punching and slapping her.

"Immediately, I just knew my life was in danger," says Kgothatso, who is now 35.

Kgothatso says she forced the passenger door open and threw herself out of the moving taxi, badly injuring her knee and causing nerve damage to her eyes. Two security guards, who were nearby, came to her aid.

She says her attacker was later jailed for a number of crimes, including what he did to her, but was released last year. Kgothatso says she now fears for her life.

Yet while Kgothatso was attacked by a stranger, according to the South African Medical Research Council, 60% of women murdered in the country between 2020-21 were killed by an intimate partner.

In the wake of her attack, Kgothatso has made changes to how she lives, including buying an imitation gun to scare off would-be attackers.

She has also stopped running alone, and insists on someone accompanying her if she goes to meet a client she hasn't met before at work.

Such precautions are all too familiar to many women in South Africa.

Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBC

Image caption,

Zama says her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles

In September police urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone, "particularly in isolated areas" - after the killing of 38-year-old mother Elizabeth Moselakgomo.

She vanished on 9 September while out running. Her badly bruised, partially clothed body was found dumped near a busy motorway in Kempton Park three days later.

It was a killing that resonated deeply within South Africa's running community, including sisters Zonke and Zama Mthethwa. They started The Pack, a women's running group in Johannesburg nine years ago. Elizabeth would sometimes attend The Pack events.

• Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South AfricaPublished19 September

• The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'Published3 October

Runners across the city joined the search efforts following Elizabeth's disappearance, and took part in protests calling for violence against women to end.

Zonke and Zama's group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles. They also get cars to follow them and have started offering self-defence coaching to the women in their running group.

"We need to try and rally and create safe spaces for women to show up authentically and to do what they love doing," says Zama, 37.

Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBC

Image caption,

Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at a prayer march to remember women who have been killed

Following her ordeal, Kgothatso moved from Kempton Park and now lives closer to her parents in another part of the country.

Her mother, a community activist, recently organised a prayer march to remember women who have been killed.

Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at the march.

Wiping away tears, she said: "To a survivor listening right now, I want to say you are not dirty, you are not broken beyond repair. You are not to blame and you are not alone."

• This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

items.title: Gisèle Pelicot 'humiliated' after nude photos sent to media to promote book
items.summary: The publisher of an essay on coercive control apologises for "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".
items.body:
Image source, EPA/Shutterstock

Image caption,

Gisèle Pelicot said she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay

ByEmer Moreau

Gisèle Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.

The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.

Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.

The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".

Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes."

"Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she said.

The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.

French media reported that Tinbad, a small Paris publishing house, emailed nude photos of Pelicot taken by her ex-husband to some media outlets in order to promote the essay.

In a statement on its website, Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation.

"We offer our sincerest apologies to Ms Gisèle Pelicot," it said. The company also apologised to the author.

Tinbad said "no images of rape or pornographic videos" were sent to the media.

French news agency AFP quoted the blurb of the book as saying coercive control was "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy".

"These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it said.

Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM the book "calls into question her status as a victim".

Prokhoris told AFP that she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher.

Fifty men were convicted alongside Pelicot's ex-husband in 2024, in a case that made her a global feminist icon.

After her husband was arrested for secretly filming underneath women's skirts in a supermarket, she discovered she had been repeatedly raped by dozens of men, including her husband, while unconscious, over a period of nearly a decade.

Pelicot said she decided to waive her right to anonymity to show how "shame has to change sides" from victims to perpetrators.

If you have been affected by the issues in this story help and support can be found at BBC Action Line.

Related topics

• Violence against women

• Sexual violence

• France

First Lady Melania Trump welcomes this year's White House Christmas tree

First Lady Melania Trump welcomes the official 2026 White House Christmas tree to the White House: It's an 18-foot (5.49 metres) concolor fir from Silent Night Evergreens, a farm in Endeavor, Wisconsin.

items.title: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
items.summary: Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were reportedly given 74 lashes in Qom.
items.body:
Image source, youtube.com/@ParastooAhmadii

Image caption,

Parastoo Ahmadi's performance was livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024

ByDavid Gritten and Ghoncheh Habibiazad, BBC Persian

A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.

Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.

Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.

This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.

In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.

At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.

There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.

On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.

"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.

"The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."

Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.

"Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).

Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.

In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".

Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.

Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.

In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.

Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.

According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.

Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.
Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.
Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.
This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.
In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.
At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.

There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.
On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.
"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.
"The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."
Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.

"Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).

Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.

In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".

Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.

Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.

In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.
Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.

According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.
Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

items.title: Comedian impersonates Trump's dance moves, mocks trade talks at Canada press dinner
items.summary: The impersonator, Canadian comedian Mark Critch, poked fun at the US president's search for a new press secretary and US-Canada trade talks.
items.body:
Figure caption,

Watch: Carney and Trump impersonators take stage with real Mark Carney

ByNadine Yousif

Senior Canada reporter

Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Canada relations and on-again, off-again trade talks.

The impersonator, played by comedian Mark Critch of the sketch comedy show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, came out after Carney jokingly pressed an "emergency comedy button" during his speech.

Critch appeared alongside another actor impersonating Carney, played by Canadian sketch comedian Mark McKinney.

"We've got two Carneys here, it's a disaster," the Trump impersonator said after he walked on stage.

Using some of Trump's signature mannerisms, like his dance moves and his slightly hunched posture, he joked about the latest US midterm elections, which led to Trump's Republican Party losing control in Congress.

"I'm so popular we just had a big BLUE WAVE in the states," the impersonator said at the Saturday press gala.

He also took aim at ongoing US-Canada trade negotiations, saying,"We're going to have a great deal. There's only one thing standing in the way: me, because I'm crazy."

There were also jabs at Trump's search for a new White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia's exit, and at US ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is unpopular among Canadians.

"I said 'find somebody who is less likeable than me,' and we got one," the Trump impersonator joked about Hoekstra.

Carney stood behind him occasionally laughing. The prime minister also delivered his own zingers, saying at one point: "This is a tough room. And I've been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator."

Both Critch and McKinney - the two impersonators - are fixtures of This Hour Has 22 Minutes, a long-standing Canadian sketch comedy show that has recently enjoyed viral internet fame for its timely skits mocking the Trump administration.

The skits, published directly on Tik Tok and YouTube, have depicted Zacharia's quick ouster, external and poked fun at rapper Nicki Minaj's, external support for Trump.

They have garnered millions of views, and even captured the attention of major US media., external

Critch and McKinney's appearance at Saturday's dinner is part of an evening of traditionally light-hearted humour, where Canadian politicians poke fun at one another at a gala hosted by the Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery.

In a separate speech, Canada's governor general, Louise Arbour, joked about Carney's popularity and frequent global travel.

"Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he's supposed to be," Arbour said.

Image source, Screengrab/CPAC

Image caption,

Comedian Mark Critch played Donald Trump during Prime Minister Mark Carney's speech at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner

items.title: 'I want to destroy capitalism, not France': On the streets with the French ultra left
items.summary: The BBC meets the far-left protesters French President Emmanuel Macron says are trying to bring down the Republic.
items.body:
Figure caption,

Watch: The BBC's Katya Adler speaks to protesters taking part in recent demonstrations

ByKatya Adler

Europe Editor

France is in turmoil. Crippling public debt, a "lame-duck" president with six months left in office, and massive social unrest - sparked by student protests which have erupted into looting and violence.

This Saturday marked the sixth weekend in a row of demos against soaring prices, worsening public services and alleged police brutality. Violence by protesters is down on last month but still present.

President Emmanuel Macron has publicly blamed riots on "delinquents" and "ultra-left groups" whose aim, he says, is to bring down the French Republic.

That's quite a claim – and one that needs examining.

The unrest in France has become a political football ahead of key presidential and parliamentary elections next year. The left in France blames the centre and right for the cost-of-living crisis that's making French people so upset and angry. They blame the hard left for fomenting violence (which they deny). While the nationalist right pledges, if elected, it will return order and security to France's streets.

So, who exactly are these "ultra-left" groups Macron speaks of? And how organised and dangerous are they?

It's infamously hard to speak to members of the radical left. They don't much like what they call mainstream media. We're viewed as part of an establishment many of them despise.

My best bet was to head out into the protests and try to approach people dressed in all black and ski masks or balaclavas (worn, they say, to hide their identity from police). It's a quasi-uniform associated with left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block.

You see them at demos all over Europe. In France, they tend to appear from city side streets, as daytime protests are dying down, dusk is falling and riot police begin to emerge in full force.

Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBC

Image caption,

The BBC's Katya Adler talking to a protester

French intelligence drastically underestimated the outpouring of anger, looting and destruction following protests last month. More than 1,000 police officers were reportedly injured, young protesters had bones broken and two reportedly lost a hand in altercations with police armed with stun grenades. Le Monde newspaper has an article, external it is constantly updating to investigate a rising number of reports of protester injuries. The French Insurers Federation estimates damages to shops and private property on 17 October alone - the day of the biggest riots - came to around €207m (£175.5m).

Since then, the French authorities are trying to tightly manage demos. Police presence is heavy. Protesters say heavy handed.

Towards the end of one of the protests this month, we saw would-be rioters vastly outnumbered, glass bottles and homemade paint bombs at the ready to throw at police. They were no match for the batons, stun grenades and tear gas the officers had to hand.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

French police pepper spraying protesters during a demonstration by French high school and university students in Paris earlier this month

As we were being forcefully kettled in by police, I tried to talk to would-be rioters. Few wanted to engage but I then met 18-year-old Nas (not his real name) and friends. They would only speak to me if they could hide their identity. This was to avoid police detection, they said.

Milling, you could say provocatively, by baton-at-the-ready police – they seemed to fit a radical-left rioter stereotype.

"How can you justify the violence?" I ask them.

"Without violence, you don't achieve anything," one of them tells me. "It's the only way to get our voices heard."

"We come from an area with a bad reputation. Our schools are a mess. Our teachers quit. You need qualifications to get a decent job. There is supposed to be equality in France. We won't give up our fight."

These young men, we discover, come from the sprawling housing estates common on French city outskirts - the banlieues - associated with deprivation, unrest and second or third generation immigrant families.

They weren't politicised or organised by the radical left, they insisted. Just angry.

Image source, Lee Durant/BBC

Image caption,

Left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block, tend to dress in all black, wearing ski masks or balaclavas

Earlier, I had spotted two hard-left student activists, standing masked on top of a bus shelter, above the thronging crowd of protesters waving banners sporting the red anarchist sign and the symbol for the Antifa (anti-fascist) movement.

I put it to them that France has a proud tradition and respect for the right to protest but that the country has been horrified by the violence it's seen over the last weeks.

They were keen to downplay the rioting but - again – would only speak if they could remain anonymous.

"Violence ends up reflecting badly on our movements. We don't like it. But what's a smashed shop window compared to police using stun guns on protesting school kids? Also, people [in France] are regularly going cold and hungry. They're losing faith in this society."

How could they believe violence would bring about a juster society, I wondered?

They shrug off my question. In France, these days, the real violence is state violence, they say.

Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBC

Image caption,

Some protesters don't support the Black Block's violence but say the state's violence is worse

French intelligence estimates there are 5,000 "ultra-left" activists in the country.

Anticapitalist Starflix (that's his codename) counts himself as one of them. The 17-year-old is also a member of the violent Black Block movement. We'd arranged to meet on the edge of the protest, by a narrow canal.

Fearful about being apprehended by police, he asked to remain anonymous.

He showed me a couple of homemade paint-bombs - eggshells filled with paint and sealed with medical tape that he throws at police officers. He carries them in his rucksack, wrapped in a royal blue Italia football shirt.

"We throw the paint bombs at the visors on riot police helmets, so they have to lift them up in order to see and that makes them suffer their own tear gas that they've sprayed at us," he tells me.

"We pick up stones and rocks too. Anything we find on the streets of Paris, to throw."

I put it to him that he and others in the Black Block are causing a lot of problems on French streets: damaging businesses, hurting police officers, destroying the demos for peaceful protesters. What is he trying to achieve?

As he's under 18, his parents give us permission to speak to him. They share his politics, Starflix tells me, but not all rioters - masked and dressed in black as he is - do.

"The Black Block isn't a single organisation. It's a technique. Some of us use violence to get government reform. I want to bring about a revolution.

"Other people are opportunists who use anonymity to steal things. When we all wear the same clothes, it makes it harder for police to identify us."

When I ask if he is scared he might get hurt or arrested, he admits he is but says what frightens him more is the thought that society might not change.

Social media plays a huge role in the riots. Starflix tells me he and his friends use Signal and Telegram to arrange to meet at protests.

Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBC

Image caption,

"The Black Block isn't a single organisation," says protester Starflix

There are numerous websites and Instagram profiles, mainly hosted by left-wing organisations, offering tips for protesters and rioters, such as: keep your phone at home so police can't track you, cover your face to avoid being identified and emulate martial arts expert Bruce Lee and "be like water" - appearing and disappearing into crowds. That's advice passed on by the Hong Kong protesters eight years ago.

While not formally organising the protests or violence with these posts, could the fact groups host this information online be viewed as a kind of incitement or manipulation of youngsters whose feelings are running so high in France?

All the young rioters I spoke to insist they are not being herded or directed, but is there something bigger behind what's happening?

Image source, Lee Durant/BBC

Image caption,

Ultra-left protesters spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymity

It takes our team a long time, but they manage to find a seasoned activist with the Black Block who would speak to us. I put to him Macron's assertion that the ultra left has organised groups that aim to bring down the French Republic. Is that true?

"It's totally false of the authorities to say we are all organised. And the intelligence services know it," the activist scoffs. "It's a manipulation of the French public to make them think there is an enemy within."

"Basically, people turn up to a protest, get dressed in black and do their own thing. The uniting factor is rage and not just in France. You see the same rage [in protests] in Italy, Germany, Spain. It's exploding by itself."

I ask if the anti-capitalist presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon and his France Unbowed party (LFI) are somehow linked to the violence. They are present at most protests, supporters handing out campaign pamphlets to the chanting crowds.

But the activist denies this, telling me Mélenchon is "a capitalist because he's part of the system". He says the LFI and the trade unions try to "calm" unrest, while he believes things need to be "stepped up a notch".

Why had he decided to talk to us, I ask - does he want to collapse the French government?

"I just want to say we don't love violence. I don't want to destroy France. We want to destroy a system that is a capitalist system, of course, but to change the society in a way that we think will be better for the most people, for more people.

"More and more find it hard to make ends meet. In the countryside, people can't even afford to fill their tank with petrol."

You have to leave the city, heading out into the gloriously autumnal French countryside, to meet some of the more organised, hardcore elements of the ultra left.

Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBC

Image caption,

Limoges Town Hall, allegedly damaged by protesters, has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in

This is a world of eco activism and known saboteurs. One man remains in police custody linked to the fire during protests at Limoges Town Hall last month. The devastated, yet somehow still elegant, 19th century building has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in. An acrid smell still hangs in the air one month on.

The 34-year-old arson suspect, who insists he's innocent, comes from a hamlet near Limoges, known for its anarchist, environmentalist community. His father, a fellow activist, is also known to French intelligence. We approached the father and the suspect's lawyer for comment. They didn't want to speak.

Instead, we met a 39-year-old father of one, a local full-time ultra-left activist for more than two decades. Like the other individuals we spoke to for this investigation, he would only talk to us on condition he could remain anonymous.

"We were all shocked by the [town hall] fire – even as we watched it happen in front of us - but it's our duty to take action," he tells me.

"I can't leave this world to my son in the state that it's in. Look how military vehicles and brute force are used by the state against our young students.

"It's amazing the people haven't taken up arms against them. Do we need a policeman killed in order for the state to listen?"

How can you say that, I want to know?

"As a child, I was educated with French values – liberty, equality, fraternity - but when I look at the social injustice in the world now, I'm disgusted. As a father, I can't let this go on. If I have to, I would take a bullet to protect the youth of this country."

These are dangerous-sounding words - but the radical left doesn't appear to be big, armed or united enough to seriously threaten France.

Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBC

Image caption,

Upcoming presidential elections offer a crossroad, with polls predicting a run-off between Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon

We repeatedly approached French intelligence. They didn't want to comment. A sign perhaps of the huge sensitivity of the current situation, especially with France hurtling towards an extremely charged presidential election.

But Michel Klein, a recently retired former police commissioner, told me he didn't think the radical left posed a serious threat to the French state.

"I believe there is a will from the radical left and the anarchists to try and destroy the Republic but they obviously don't have the means to do it," he told me.

He sees no risk of civil war in France (a possibility you hear some in the country discuss these days) but he identified a rising risk of clashes between far-left and far-right groups ahead of the presidential election.

Polls currently predict a run-off in the vote between nationalist candidate Marine Le Pen and anticapitalist Mélenchon.

Far-right vigilante groups have begun appearing on the edge of protests in a number of cities across France to "protect French streets", they say.

The popular hard-left presidential candidate Mélenchon attends most demos, his supporters handing political pamphlets to the chanting crowds, but he denies any links with violence.

France is so polarised, there's little sign next year's presidential vote will calm things. This turbulent mix of left and right, social and political unrest, feels like a perfect storm.

Related topics

• France

• Emmanuel Macron

• French politics

More on this story

But the activist denies this, telling me Mélenchon is "a capitalist because he's part of the system". He says the LFI and the trade unions try to "calm" unrest, while he believes things need to be "stepped up a notch".
Why had he decided to talk to us, I ask - does he want to collapse the French government?

"I just want to say we don't love violence. I don't want to destroy France. We want to destroy a system that is a capitalist system, of course, but to change the society in a way that we think will be better for the most people, for more people.
"More and more find it hard to make ends meet. In the countryside, people can't even afford to fill their tank with petrol."
You have to leave the city, heading out into the gloriously autumnal French countryside, to meet some of the more organised, hardcore elements of the ultra left.

blocks.alt: Limoges town hall is seen with extensive fire damage and scaffolding going up

blocks.text: Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBC
Image caption,
Limoges Town Hall, allegedly damaged by protesters, has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in

This is a world of eco activism and known saboteurs. One man remains in police custody linked to the fire during protests at Limoges Town Hall last month. The devastated, yet somehow still elegant, 19th century building has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in. An acrid smell still hangs in the air one month on.

The 34-year-old arson suspect, who insists he's innocent, comes from a hamlet near Limoges, known for its anarchist, environmentalist community. His father, a fellow activist, is also known to French intelligence. We approached the father and the suspect's lawyer for comment. They didn't want to speak.

Instead, we met a 39-year-old father of one, a local full-time ultra-left activist for more than two decades. Like the other individuals we spoke to for this investigation, he would only talk to us on condition he could remain anonymous.
"We were all shocked by the [town hall] fire – even as we watched it happen in front of us - but it's our duty to take action," he tells me.
"I can't leave this world to my son in the state that it's in. Look how military vehicles and brute force are used by the state against our young students.
"It's amazing the people haven't taken up arms against them. Do we need a policeman killed in order for the state to listen?"
How can you say that, I want to know?

"As a child, I was educated with French values – liberty, equality, fraternity - but when I look at the social injustice in the world now, I'm disgusted. As a father, I can't let this go on. If I have to, I would take a bullet to protect the youth of this country."
These are dangerous-sounding words - but the radical left doesn't appear to be big, armed or united enough to seriously threaten France.

blocks.alt: A French street sign is seen with graffiti reading "revolte" after the word "nation".

blocks.text: Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBC
Image caption,
Upcoming presidential elections offer a crossroad, with polls predicting a run-off between Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon

We repeatedly approached French intelligence. They didn't want to comment. A sign perhaps of the huge sensitivity of the current situation, especially with France hurtling towards an extremely charged presidential election.
But Michel Klein, a recently retired former police commissioner, told me he didn't think the radical left posed a serious threat to the French state.
"I believe there is a will from the radical left and the anarchists to try and destroy the Republic but they obviously don't have the means to do it," he told me.

He sees no risk of civil war in France (a possibility you hear some in the country discuss these days) but he identified a rising risk of clashes between far-left and far-right groups ahead of the presidential election.
Polls currently predict a run-off in the vote between nationalist candidate Marine Le Pen and anticapitalist Mélenchon.
Far-right vigilante groups have begun appearing on the edge of protests in a number of cities across France to "protect French streets", they say.
The popular hard-left presidential candidate Mélenchon attends most demos, his supporters handing political pamphlets to the chanting crowds, but he denies any links with violence.
France is so polarised, there's little sign next year's presidential vote will calm things. This turbulent mix of left and right, social and political unrest, feels like a perfect storm.

items.title: Ukraine shares video of strikes on Russian ships off Libya
items.summary: President Zelensky said a Russia warship was sunk, with a Russian cargo ship also hit.
items.body:
Ukraine shares video of strikes on Russian ships off Libya

Ukraine shares video of strikes on Russian ships off Libya

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has shared footage on social media which he says shows strikes on Russian vessels off the coast of Libya on Sunday.

A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones and the attack also targeted a second vessel, a cargo ship which was being used to transport weapons, Zelensky said.

Footage verified by the BBC shows a ship ablaze at Benghazi's port.

The local health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.

Following the strikes, the Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.
